$comment: The protocol version both sides must agree on, plus conformance cases for the `GET /api/v1/version` payload. `protocol_version` is the assertion that matters: server/tests/test_protocol_fixtures.py checks it against fenixspoon.protocol.PROTOCOL_VERSION and the SDK's conformance suite checks it against PROTOCOL_VERSION in @fenix-spoon/client, so bumping one side without the other fails CI on the other. 1.1 added vector fields to both result kinds; 1.2 added the discovery operations (/environment, /capabilities, /capabilities/{name}, /capabilities/{name}/schema) and their payloads — both additive, so 1.0, 1.1 and 1.2 share /api/v1. 1.3 added `metrics` and `diagnostics` to the result envelope, plus the compact `/jobs/{id}/summary` and `/jobs/{id}/query` routes; the heat adapters' `t_max` and `t_rise` moved out of `stats` into `metrics` in the same bump, which is additive because `stats` keys have always been documented as server-defined and all optional. 1.4 added the content-addressed result cache (#47): `provenance` on the result envelope and as a compact level, `cached` on the submit response, and real cache state in `environment.inspect`. Additive, but note one behavioural change a client can see — `POST /jobs` may return a job that is already `done`. 1.5 added the `series1d` result kind and the `series` key beside `data` (#69), the `assumptions` section on `capability.describe` (#70), and the `series` level on `/jobs/{id}/summary`; the potential-flow adapters gained `circulation`, `c_l`, `c_m_c4` and `x_cp` in the same release (#68), which needs no bump of its own because `metrics` keys have always been whatever a capability declares. It is 1.5 rather than a second 1.4 because #47 reached main first and the rule below applies to it as much as to 1.2. Unlike the 1.2 discovery payloads, the series half *is* validated on both sides: a curve has a browser consumer, so there is a second implementation to drift from — and `series_limits` in results.json pins its ceilings the way `protocol_version` pins this. The `workspace` path in the environment payload is part of 1.2 rather than a 1.3: #43 specified the field and had nothing to point at, #44 built the workspace, and both land unreleased on the same branch. Folding it in is only correct while 1.2 is unmerged — once a version is on main it is fixed, and the next addition is a bump. When a MAJOR arrives, this file gains a `superseded` list and the corpus holds cases for both. 1.6 added `over` to a declared metric (#86): `payload` (the default, and what every steady capability means) or `run` for a quantity only the adapter can supply — a peak over a transient's history, a time to reach a level. Additive, and a discovery-payload change like 1.2's, so the SDK carries the version but models nothing new. 1.7 gave an artifact an optional `t` and the result envelope a derived `frames` list (#86): the time index of a transient is the artifacts carrying an instant, in time order. Additive, and deliberately not a new result kind — the field history crosses as references like every other large thing, and there is no server-side reduction at a chosen instant. Deriving the index from the files rather than storing it beside them is what makes a frame naming a file the result does not serve unrepresentable. Unlike 1.6, the SDK does model this one: `ArtifactRef.t` and `FrameRef` are part of the result envelope it already types, so leaving them out would have made the version constant advertise a shape the types denied. 1.8 let a geometry *name* pieces of its boundary (#85): optional stable `point_ids` on a polygon, and a `boundaries` list whose selectors are topological (`part`), by point id, or geometric (`near`/`box`/`all_of`). Additive and empty by default — every adapter shipped today puts its conditions where the outer/obstacle split implies them. Ids and predicates are both here because they follow different things: an id follows the shape through an edit, a predicate follows the space. What happens *on* a named boundary is a load case, and lands separately. 1.9 said what happens *on* a named boundary, which 1.8 could only point at (#85): a `load_case` workspace object whose body is `{boundary: {key: value}}`, `conditions` on a submission for the inline form, and a `conditions` section on `capability.describe` listing the keys a capability reads and their units. Additive on the wire, and the values are an open map of scalars exactly like `Region2D.material` — a typed enum of condition kinds would put physics into the protocol and make every new physics a protocol change. What keeps that openness honest is the capability declaration: a key nothing declares, or a boundary the geometry does not name, is a 422 at submit rather than a silent no-op, and all three refusals are in errors.json with the rest of the partition. Two things a caller should know beyond the additions. The `load_case` object body is now *validated*, where before it was stored as given — the same tightening #48 applied to `study`, and the same reasoning: a body gets a schema at the moment something reads it. And a load case is part of a solve's content address, so two load cases on one shape are two cache entries; leaving them out would have served the clamped answer to the caller who asked about the free one. The SDK models this one rather than merely tracking it, as it did for 1.7 and for the same reason: `JobRequest` is a shape it already types, and a version constant that advertised `conditions` while the types denied it would be the drift this file exists to prevent. 1.10 bound the workspace to HTTP (ADR 0002): objects as a resource collection under /objects/{type}/{id} with the revision as a query parameter, and `design` on a job submission so a browser can solve by reference rather than resending its geometry. Additive — every route is new and `POST /jobs` still accepts the inline form — so 1.10 shares /api/v1 with 1.0. Note the version string itself: this is the first minor that breaks both a float comparison and a lexicographic one, and the corpus carries a case for it above. 1.11 added the two study routes (ADR 0002 decision 3): POST /studies/{id}/run and GET /studies/{id}. A study is an object that runs rather than an endpoint that computes, so there is no request body — everything the run needs is in the revision it names. Both take `?revision=` for the same reason the object routes do, and it is not decoration: "you cannot pin it" is the first thing the ADR holds against a sweep posted as a body, so a binding that could only act on the head would refute its own argument. Additive. 1.12 finished ADR 0002 with the optimization routes (decision 4): POST /optimizations/{id}/run and GET /optimizations/{id}, the same object-that-runs shape. One shipped behaviour changed with it, and it is the only non-additive-feeling part of an additive bump: `optimize.run` used to block for the whole search and return the finished report, which HTTP cannot do, so it returns a receipt on every transport now and the waiting moved to the CLI and the Python API — the pattern `job.submit` has always had. The search continues as a task owned by the server process, which is the first thing here that is neither a job nor a request; it is a driver and not state, so a restart costs a loop and nothing else. The report gains `running`, which is process-local and says so. 1.13 added the `axisymmetric2d` geometry kind (#100): a meridian (r, z) half-section of a body of revolution, and the first new member of the geometry union since `regions2d`. Additive — a new member of a discriminated union, so a client that never sends one is unaffected. It is a filled region map like `regions2d`, and shares that kind's rules by sharing the function that enforces them rather than by restating them; two rules are its own, and both follow from what the coordinates mean. `rmin >= 0`, because a negative radius is not a domain a body of revolution has — it is a plane section that has been mislabelled. And a region may lie *on* r = 0 when the section reaches the axis, because a solid shaft is bounded by it and the strictly-inside rule would otherwise make the commonest axisymmetric shape unrepresentable. What the kind buys is a **refusal**: the same rectangle could always be sent as `regions2d` with bounds starting at zero and *meant* as r, and a plane solver would accept it and quietly solve a slice — a wrong number rather than an error. `geometry_types` and the 422 behind it are what make the two readings distinguishable, which is why this is a discriminator and not a convention. The axis itself needed no mechanism: in an r-weighted weak form the boundary term carries the same r and vanishes at r = 0, so the natural symmetry condition is what an adapter gets by doing nothing there, and a caller wanting to *name* the axis uses the `near` selector 1.8 already shipped. A section that does not reach the axis is legitimate — the motivating sensor's does not — and the geometry corpus carries one so no solver may assume otherwise. Landed with two adapters that read it, `mock.electrostatics_axi2d` and `dolfinx.electrostatics_axi2d`, following this repository's rule for the domain contract: the capability first, the protocol change second. The SDK models this one rather than merely tracking it, as it did for 1.7 and 1.9: the geometry union is a shape it already types, and the corpus is shared, so a payload this server refuses must not be one the SDK's validator builds. 1.14 gave an artifact an optional `mode` and the result envelope a derived `modes` list (#101): the mode index of an eigensolve is the artifacts carrying a mode number, in mode order — 1.7's design for time, applied to an ordering that is not time. Additive. **What it decides is that this is a second field rather than a reuse of `t`** (ADR 0004). `t` is an instant in the solver's time unit; a mode number is an ordinal with no metric on it, so one slot for both would make a viewer's time slider read "mode 3" as three seconds and leave every consumer of 1.7 asking which meaning a given result meant. The two are mutually exclusive on one file and the model refuses the combination rather than picking one — a file holds an instant or a mode, and a result that indexed it twice would order it two ways. What the eigensolve needed *beyond* this was nothing, which is the finding #101 predicted: the spectrum is a `series1d`, the row of that model's own table of purposes ("where does it resonate?") that had had no producer since 1.5, and its abscissa is the mode number — so a frequency and a shape are joined by that number rather than by position in two lists that happen to be ordered alike. Landed with `mock.modal2d` and `dolfinx.modal2d` on the same rule as 1.13: the capability first, the protocol change second. The SDK models this one as it modelled 1.7's `t`, because the result envelope is a shape it already types and a version constant advertising an index the types denied would be the drift this file exists to prevent. 1.15 gave `environment.inspect` a `plugins` list (#105): the third-party adapter sources this server read, and what each one did. Additive, and a discovery-payload change like 1.2's and 1.6's, so the SDK carries the version but models nothing new — the environment payload is not a shape it types. What it exists for is the half of ADR 0005 decision 5 that had no outlet: breadth is supposed to be bought with adapters rather than with protocol, and until #105 there was no supported way to load an adapter that does not live in this repository, so every new physics had to land here. Two sources now do it — an entry point in the `fenixspoon.solvers` group, and `FENIXSPOON_SOLVER_MODULES` for an adapter not worth packaging — both loaded after the built-ins, so a plugin cannot take a shipped name by importing first. The reason any of it reaches the wire is that a missing capability is otherwise a refusal with no reason: a caller that does not find a capability cannot tell "not installed" from "installed and raised ImportError", and only one of those is a broken deployment. So a load that fails is reported with its exception text rather than propagated (one stranger's bad import is not this server's outage) and a loader switched off with `FENIXSPOON_DISABLE_PLUGINS` reports a `disabled` entry rather than an empty list, because "off" and "none installed" are different answers. What a plugin deliberately cannot do is add a geometry kind, a result kind or a field: an adapter chooses from the vocabulary the protocol already has, or it comes here and argues for more. That is ADR 0005's admission test keeping its own back door shut. 1.16 gave a capability a `convergence` declaration and a result an `iterations` count (#107). Additive, and a discovery-payload change like 1.2's, 1.6's and 1.15's, so the SDK carries the version but models nothing new. What it fixes is a half-shipped vocabulary: `converged`, `residual` and `warnings` have been on a result since 1.3 and the iterative adapters set them, but nothing declared what any of it meant — so `residual` was a bare float that is a temperature change per sweep in one adapter and a dimensionless relative residual in another, and a caller could not tell whether a null `converged` meant "direct solve" or "nobody said". The reason it went unnoticed for seven adapter pairs is that none of them was nonlinear: every operator shipped before #107 is independent of its own solution, so the vocabulary was never under load. **The load-bearing field is `on_failure`**, which says what a caller receives when the tolerance is not reached: `return` (the result comes back with `converged: false` and a warning) or `fail` (the job fails). Both are correct and the difference is not strictness — a relaxation sweep stopped at its cap is a legitimate preview, while a Newton iterate short of tolerance solves a problem with the wrong coefficients, and returning that with a quiet flag is the plausible-looking answer this contract exists to prevent. It is enforced rather than documented: a capability declaring `fail` that returns an unconverged result fails the job, the same shape of refusal `MetricSpec.over` makes in 1.6. Landed with `mock.heat_nonlinear2d` and `dolfinx.heat_nonlinear2d` on the rule this repository follows for the domain contract: the capability first, the protocol change second. They are the first pair here whose operator depends on its own solution, held to the Kirchhoff closed form for a slab rather than only to each other, because Picard and Newton converge to the same fixed point instead of bracketing it from opposite sides.

valid.name: a later minor on the same major
valid.$comment: Additive, so a 1.0 client must still accept it.

valid.name: a two-digit minor
valid.$comment: 1.10, and the first case in this corpus that exists to break naive comparisons rather than to exercise a shape. As a float it parses to 1.1 and sorts below 1.9; as a string it *also* sorts below "1.9", because '1' < '9' at the third character. The document has warned about the first since 1.0 and not about the second, and a draft of ADR 0002 proposed pinning `"1.10" > "1.9"` as a test — an assertion that is false, written by someone who had read the warning. Split on the dot and compare the halves as integers, which is what checkProtocolCompatibility does.

invalid.name: missing protocol
invalid.reason: protocol is required: a payload that cannot say what it speaks is useless

invalid.name: missing api_path
invalid.reason: api_path is required so a client can confirm where this version is served

invalid.name: protocol as a number
invalid.reason: MAJOR.MINOR is a string; as a float 1.10 would compare below 1.9. Note pydantic v2 refuses this on type alone — it does not coerce numbers to str — so this case guards the rule, not a coercion bug.

invalid.name: protocol with a non-numeric minor
invalid.reason: MAJOR.MINOR must be two integers; '1.banana' cannot be compared with anything

invalid.name: protocol with only a major
invalid.reason: '1' leaves the minor implicit, and an implicit minor is a guess
